Make a two-column chart. Column 1: Details about how camp is organized (cabins, tables, who sits where). Column 2: What this shows about camp expectations, values, and traditions. Write at least three rows, citing the page for each."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"When we cite evidence, we do two jobs. First, we point to exactly what the text says. Second, we explain what we infer from it. A detail like \"campers sit by cabin\" only helps us if we say what it shows about the camp."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"I notice in cabin eleven that Luke explains who stays there, and the cabin is crowded. That tells me something about how the camp treats campers whose godly parent has not claimed them yet. I'll record the detail, the page, and what I infer."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Luke's conversation with Percy in cabin eleven show about how camp is organized?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On p. 100, Luke shows Percy to cabin eleven and explains that it is Hermes's cabin. It shows that campers live by the god they are connected to, and that Hermes's cabin takes in campers who haven't been claimed yet. That tells me the camp makes room for everyone, even people who don't know where they belong."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do the details about the cabins and the tables at the pavilion show about the camp's expectations for campers?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"At dinner the campers line up and sit at tables by cabin. That shows they follow a routine and are part of a group. It also shows each cabin has its own place and belongs to a larger community. Sitting with cabin eleven shows Percy has a place now."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"On pp. 102–103 Luke and others mention *quests*, *prophecies*, and a *centaur* and *nymphs* at the pavilion. What do these show about what life at camp is like?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They show that camp life isn't ordinary. Campers go on quests and hear prophecies, and mythical creatures like nymphs and a centaur are part of everyday life. Camp is a place where being a demigod is normal, which is what Percy never had before."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do these traditions echo ancient myths?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In ancient Greek myths, heroes went on quests, people listened to prophecies, and gods like Hermes were linked to certain groups, like travelers. The camp uses the same ideas, like honoring the gods and welcoming travelers and strangers, so it feels like a living version of the old stories."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1"],"stem":"Which detail from Chapter 7 best supports the idea that Camp Half-Blood welcomes newcomers, including campers who have not been claimed?","choices":[{"text":"Luke takes Percy to cabin eleven and explains that Hermes's cabin makes room for campers who are not yet claimed.","correct":true,"rationale":"This detail shows the camp has a place for newcomers and campers who don't yet know their godly parent, which supports the idea of welcome."},{"text":"The campers line up before dinner in order of their cabin numbers.","correct":false,"rationale":"This shows the camp is organized and has routines, but it does not directly show welcome toward unclaimed newcomers."},{"text":"Campers go on quests that sometimes put them in danger.","correct":false,"rationale":"Quests are part of camp life, but danger doesn't show how the camp welcomes newcomers. Students may confuse an interesting detail with relevant evidence."},{"text":"The pavilion is outdoors with a view of the water.","correct":false,"rationale":"The setting is part of the description, but it does not show how newcomers are treated."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in citing details and explaining what they show about camp organization and values. Language focus: citing evidence, explaining inferences, expanded noun phrases.","sayAsk":"Say: Let's find the detail first, then explain it. Ask: What does the text say? What does that show about the camp? Frames: On page ___, the text says ___. This shows that camp values ___ because ___. For noun phrases: Add a describing word to the noun: a *crowded* cabin, a *welcoming* community, an *old* tradition. You said \"camp is nice\" — we can say \"the camp is a *welcoming community* that makes room for every camper.\"","watchFor":"If students retell the scene without explaining it, then prompt: \"What does that detail show about what the camp values?\" If students copy a long quotation, then prompt them to paraphrase in a short phrase and add the page. Success looks like a cited detail paired with an explanation using \"this shows that.\""},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: connecting a detail to a value","tryThis":"Give a sentence starter chart: Detail → \"This shows camp values ___.\" Provide a word bank (welcome, belonging, respect, tradition, family, community) and model one row with the whole class."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to choose one camp practice and write a sentence explaining what ancient Greek tradition it echoes and why Riordan might include that echo."}]}]},{"id":"lia-closing-episode","title":"Part B: How Does This Section Close Percy's First Day?","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.5","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 7","pages":"pp. 100–106"},{"type":"directions","text":"Create a four-box sequence organizer: 1) cabin eleven, 2) the pavilion dinner, 3) offerings to the gods, 4) the campfire sing-along. In each box write what happens and one detail from the text. Then, with a partner, discuss how these four parts work together as the last episode of Percy's first day."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Authors build stories in chapters and scenes. A scene can open a new part of the story, build tension, or bring one part to an end. To analyze structure, ask: What came before this scene? What does this scene add? How does it help close a part of the plot?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Remember Lesson 12: Percy arrives hurt, grieving, and confused. Everything that came before has been about getting to camp and surviving. Let's see how pp. 100–106 finish that story arc."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is the order of events from cabin eleven to the end of the chapter?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"First Percy goes to cabin eleven and talks with Luke. Then the campers go to dinner at the pavilion. Next they make offerings to the gods by burning food. Finally everyone gathers around the campfire for a sing-along."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does this sequence work as the closing episode of Percy's first day at camp?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It starts with Percy learning where he will stay, moves through a meal and a ritual, and ends with a calm group song at night. That feels like the end of a day, and it ends peacefully after all the danger earlier. Percy goes from stranger to someone who takes part in what everyone does."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does this section help conclude the \"arrival at camp\" arc?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The arrival arc is about Percy getting to camp and finding out whether he belongs. These pages answer that by showing him with a cabin, a table, a ritual, and a campfire with others. By the end he is part of the camp, so the arrival part of the story is finished and the next chapters can move on to training."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate and listen for students who say \"it's the end of the day\" but stop there. Push them to name what changes for Percy, from outsider to participant, and to cite a detail."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining how scenes fit together to close a part of the story. Language focus: sequence words and structure vocabulary.","sayAsk":"Say: Let's use sequence words to retell, then explain why the ending matters. Frames: First ___, next ___, then ___, finally ___. This section closes the arrival arc because ___. Before this, Percy ___; now Percy ___. Rehearse with a partner in the home language, then restate in English.","watchFor":"If students only list events, then prompt: \"What does the order of events show about how Percy's day ends?\" If students are unsure of 'arc,' then explain it as the 'shape' of one part of the story, with a beginning, middle, and end. Success looks like students using sequence words and a because-statement about the closing."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: explaining how a section fits the overall structure","tryThis":"Provide a Before / Now frame: \"Before this section, Percy ___. In this section, he ___. So the section closes the arc by ___.\" Complete the first one together."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to predict how the next arc (training and quests) will differ from the arrival arc, and to explain how this ending sets that change up."}]}]},{"id":"lia-figurative-mood","title":"Part C: How Does Language Create a Welcoming Mood?","minutes":10,"standards":["L.6.5.a","RL.6.1","RL.6.5"],"routine":"Annotation and Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 7","pages":"pp. 100–106"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread the passages about the goblet that fills magically, the smoke from the offerings that smells like favorite foods, and the campfire scene. Annotate: underline descriptive words and images; circle any figurative language (such as personification, where something non-human acts or feels like a person). In the margin, write the feeling each passage creates. Then complete the Quick Write."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Descriptive language uses details that help us see, smell, hear, or feel a scene. Figurative language, like personification, says something that isn't literally true to make a stronger picture. Both shape the mood, which is the feeling readers get from the text."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Take the smoke on p. 104. The smell of the burning food is not just a smell. If it reminds Percy of favorite foods, it brings comfort and memory. Let's name the mood together."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do the magically filling goblet and the smoke that smells like favorite foods affect the mood?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The goblet fills with whatever Percy wants, and the smoke smells like his favorite foods. These details make camp feel generous and caring, like the place is looking out for him. The mood is warm and comforting."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In the campfire scene, which words or images help create the mood? If the fire seems to respond to the campers' feelings, what figurative language is that?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The warm glow, the songs, and everyone gathered together create a cozy mood. If the fire reacts to the campers' feelings, that is personification because the fire acts like a person. It shows that the whole place shares the campers' happiness."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does this language deepen Percy's sense that he has finally found a home?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The food, the smells, and the songs are what make a home feel like home. When Percy gets comfort and a place with others, he feels safe and wanted. The language shows he belongs instead of just telling us."},{"type":"directions","text":"Quick Write (3–4 sentences): Explain how Riordan's word choice and imagery in pp. 100–106 create a warm, welcoming mood. Include at least one cited detail, name the figurative language or imagery, and use one expanded noun phrase (for example, *the warm, flickering campfire*)."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["L.6.5.a","RL.6.4"],"stem":"In Chapter 7, the smoke from the offerings smells like Percy's favorite foods. What is the main effect of this detail?","choices":[{"text":"It creates a comforting, welcoming mood and makes camp feel like home to Percy.","correct":true,"rationale":"The familiar smells connect camp to comfort and memory, which supports the warm mood and Percy's sense of belonging."},{"text":"It shows the gods are angry at the campers' offerings.","correct":false,"rationale":"Nothing in the text suggests anger. The scene is pleasant, so this misreads the gods' response."},{"text":"It tells readers that the food at camp is poisoned.","correct":false,"rationale":"This invents a threat. The smell is pleasant, and the scene is about comfort."},{"text":"It proves that Percy's offerings are all the same as the other campers'.","correct":false,"rationale":"The detail is about Percy's personal favorite foods and the mood, not whether the offerings are identical."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in interpreting imagery and personification and in expanding noun phrases to describe mood. Language focus: sensory adjectives, expanded noun phrases, and evaluating language choices.","sayAsk":"Say: Find words that help you see, smell, or feel the scene. Ask: Which word makes the mood feel warm? Why is that a good word choice here? Frames: The author uses the word/phrase ___ to show ___. This creates a ___ mood because ___. Expand noun phrases: the *smoke* → the *sweet, curling smoke*; the *fire* → the *warm, glowing campfire*. (Emerging: add one sensory adjective. Expanding: add two or a comparative. Bridging: add a clause such as \"the fire that glowed with the campers' songs.\")","watchFor":"If students name the mood only as 'good' or 'happy,' then prompt: \"Find a more precise word, such as cozy, comforting, or welcoming, and point to the detail that shows it.\" If students call all description figurative language, then ask: \"Could this literally happen? Is the writer comparing or giving human traits?\" Success looks like students naming the mood precisely, identifying one figure of speech, and writing at least one expanded noun phrase."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: interpreting figurative language in context","tryThis":"Use a three-step prompt: 1) What does the sentence literally say? 2) Is it comparing or giving human traits to a non-human thing? 3) What feeling does it create? Provide a word bank of mood words (cozy, warm, comforting, welcoming, peaceful)."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to rewrite one passage in a flat, neutral way, then explain how the mood changes. Or have them find a second figurative device and explain its effect on Percy's feeling of home."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students pull together what camp life shows about community values and how Riordan's language creates a feeling of home.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-reflection","title":"Values, Traditions, and Home","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.5","L.6.5.a"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"In the performance task, you will analyze the values in a community's stories and traditions and use details from the text as evidence. The details about ___ show that camp values ___. The author's language, such as ___, creates a ___ mood, which shows that Percy ___.*"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Chapter 7 closes Percy's first day at camp by moving from cabin eleven to dinner, the offerings, and the campfire. The details about the tables and cabins show that camp values belonging and tradition. The author's language, such as the smoke that smells like favorite foods, creates a warm mood, which shows that Percy feels at home for the first time."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Collect or glance at responses as an exit check. Look for a cited detail, a named value, and a precisely named mood. Use what you see to plan small groups for Flex Days."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (Optional)","purpose":"Students preview the next chapter and practice annotating for details about how Percy changes.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-ch8","title":"Read and Annotate Chapter 8","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.10"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 8","pages":"pp. 107–116"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read and annotate *The Lightning Thief*, Chapter 8 (pp. 107–116).
